prompt: Why does every program in this lesson keep the 50 test tickets out of what a method may learn from?
hint: Think about what the score is supposed to tell you.

choices.text: Because embedding all 150 tickets at once would go past the model's 256-piece limit
choices.why: The 256-piece limit applies to one text, not to a batch; tickets.py embeds each split in one call without trouble.

choices.text: Because the test tickets carry no label in the file
choices.why: They carry one, as the head of the file shows; the label is what the score is counted against.

choices.text: So that the score says how the method handles messages it has never seen
choices.why: Right. A method scored on tickets it learned from is scored on its memory, which says nothing about tomorrow's messages.

choices.text: So that k-nearest neighbours has fewer tickets to compare and runs faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it. The split exists so that the measurement is honest.

prompt: `knn.py` computes `S = Xte @ Xtr.T` with 50 test tickets and 100 training tickets. How many dot products does that one line compute?
hint: One for every pair of a test ticket and a training ticket.

prompt: k-NN scored 46 of 50 with `k=1` and 42 with `k=3`. How can three neighbours do worse than one?
hint: A vote changes nothing while the neighbours agree.

choices.text: With `k=3` the vectors are averaged before comparing, which blurs them
choices.why: Nothing is averaged in knn.py; the labels of the nearest k are counted, and the vectors are left as they are.

choices.text: With `k=3` each test ticket is compared with only three training tickets
choices.why: Every test ticket is still compared with all 100; k only decides how many of the nearest are counted.

choices.text: A larger `k` uses a less precise number type for the scores
choices.why: The scores are the same float32 dot products for every k; only the vote changes.

choices.text: When the three disagree, two tickets further away outvote the nearest one
choices.why: Right. With k=1 the nearest ticket decides alone; with k=3 a pair of further tickets with another label wins the count.

prompt: Marginalia decides that from next month every refund request, for a printed book or an e-book, goes to a new refunds desk. What does the k-NN classifier in this lesson need?
hint: Separate what the vectors hold from what the labels hold.

choices.text: Every ticket embedded again, because the vectors were computed with the old labels
choices.why: The embedding model never saw a label. The vectors describe the text, and the text has not changed.

choices.text: The stored refund tickets relabelled; no vector changes and nothing is trained
choices.why: Right. k-NN copies labels from stored tickets. Relabel those, and new refund tickets get the new desk from their neighbours; the vectors never depended on the labels.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because the refund tickets are already close to each other
choices.why: Being close is why they will move together, but they move to whatever label they carry; until they are relabelled they carry the old ones.

choices.text: A new embedding model trained on refund tickets until they form their own cluster
choices.why: The refund tickets already sit together, as t054's neighbours showed; what is missing is a label, not a model.

prompt: Giving a ticket the most frequent label among the k closest labelled tickets is called k-nearest ___.
hint: The closest tickets are next door to it.

prompt: Why does `centroids.py` divide each centroid by its own length before comparing?
hint: Lesson 2's trap with vectors of different lengths.

choices.text: Because NumPy's `mean` returns a vector 384 times too large
choices.why: The mean is a correct average; it comes out shorter than 1, not larger, because the vectors point in different directions.

choices.text: So that no desk wins dot products just because its average came out longer
choices.why: Right. After the division all five centroids have length 1, and the dot product compares directions only.

choices.text: To turn the five scores into probabilities that add up to 1
choices.why: That is what logistic regression does with its scores. A normalised centroid still gives cosines, which do not add up to anything.

choices.text: Because the ticket vectors were not of length 1 to begin with
choices.why: Every vector from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 has length 1; it is their average that does not.

prompt: Before renormalising, the returns centroid had length 0.592 and the payments centroid 0.526. What does the difference say?
hint: Twenty arrows added up: when is the sum longest?

choices.text: Returns has more training tickets than payments
choices.why: Both have 20. The mean divides by the count, so the count does not set the length anyway.

choices.text: The payments tickets are shorter texts
choices.why: Every ticket vector has length 1 whatever the length of its text; the centroid's length comes from the directions.

choices.text: The returns centroid will win more comparisons after renormalising
choices.why: After renormalising all five have length 1, which is the point of doing it; the old length no longer counts.

choices.text: Returns tickets point in more similar directions
choices.why: Right. Vectors that agree add up to a longer average; the more varied a desk, the shorter its centroid.

prompt: Two unit vectors have a dot product of 0.5. What is the length of their average, to three decimals?
hint: The squared length of a + b is a·a + 2a·b + b·b. Then halve the length.

prompt: `centroids.py` also prints, for each desk, the training ticket furthest from that desk's centroid. What is that list good for?
hint: Why do you need my date of birth? was the furthest account ticket.

choices.text: A list for a person to check
choices.why: Right. The least typical tickets are where a wrong label or a desk that is really two groups shows up first.

choices.text: Deleting those tickets automatically, because they lower the accuracy
choices.why: Nothing showed they lower it, and the date-of-birth ticket was correctly labelled; deleting unusual examples throws away exactly the cases that are hard.

choices.text: Choosing each desk's prototype for the report
choices.why: The prototype is the nearest ticket, the most typical one; the furthest is the opposite.

choices.text: Choosing the value of `k` for k-nearest neighbours
choices.why: k is chosen by measuring accuracy at several values, as knn.py did; the centroid distances say nothing about it.

prompt: A logistic regression like the one in `trained.py` is trained on WordLlama's 256-number vectors to sort tickets into six desks. How many numbers does it learn?
hint: One weight per coordinate per desk, and one constant per desk.

prompt: On MiniLM's vectors, logistic regression and centroids both scored 47 of 50. Which explanation fits what the lesson measured?
hint: Look at what the embedding had already done before training started.

choices.text: Logistic regression ignores the vectors and reads the words of each ticket
choices.why: It only ever sees the 384 numbers per ticket; it has no access to the words.

choices.text: `max_iter=1000` stopped the training before it had finished
choices.why: max_iter is a ceiling raised so that the solver can finish; it finished, in milliseconds, without a warning.

choices.text: The vectors already separate the desks, and 20 tickets a desk leave little to learn
choices.why: Right. A learned weighting can only fix what the space gets wrong, and here it gets little wrong; with weaker vectors the gap opened.

choices.text: A trained model and a centroid always tie when every desk has the same number of tickets
choices.why: On WordLlama's vectors with 20 per desk, also balanced, they scored 44 and 42.

prompt: On WordLlama's vectors with 20 tickets per desk, the nearest neighbour scored 40, centroids 42 and logistic regression 44. What does that support?
hint: Compare it with the same row for MiniLM, where the three scored 46, 47 and 47.

choices.text: WordLlama is a better model than MiniLM for classifying tickets
choices.why: Every WordLlama score is below the MiniLM score for the same method; it is the weaker of the two here.

choices.text: Learned weights help more when the vectors separate less well
choices.why: Right. On MiniLM's sharper vectors the three were within one ticket; on WordLlama's, training gained two over the centroids.

choices.text: Logistic regression needs fewer examples than centroids do
choices.why: The table says otherwise: with 2 per desk on WordLlama, centroids scored 39 and logistic regression 36.

choices.text: A static model cannot be used for nearest-neighbour classification
choices.why: It was used: 40 of 50 is a working classifier, only a weaker one.

prompt: The team wants tickets the classifier is unsure about to go to a person instead of a desk. t027 got 0.388 for payments and 0.368 for shipping. What should they do?
hint: A probability from this model is a ranking of its confidence.

choices.text: Send every ticket under 0.5 to a person, because below that the model is wrong more often than right
choices.why: That reads the probability as a promise of accuracy, which nobody measured; with five desks a top probability under 0.5 can still be right most of the time.

choices.text: Switch to k-nearest neighbours, which reports its confidence more precisely
choices.why: k-NN as written here returns a label and nothing else; it reports no confidence at all.

choices.text: Train again until every test ticket's top probability is above 0.9
choices.why: Training on the test tickets until they look certain is learning from the test set; the scores would then measure memory.

choices.text: Choose a cut-off from how often low-probability tickets are wrong on held-out labelled data
choices.why: Right. Whether 0.388 is low enough to worry about is a measurement on your own data, like any threshold.

prompt: Which method of this lesson is zero-shot classification, as `zeroshot.py` does it, closest to?
hint: What are the five vectors each ticket is compared with?

choices.text: Logistic regression, with the descriptions used as learned weights
choices.why: Nothing is learned in zeroshot.py: the descriptions are embedded and compared by dot product, with no weights fitted.

choices.text: k-nearest neighbours with `k=5`, one neighbour per desk
choices.why: k-NN with k=5 takes the five nearest training tickets, which may all be from one desk; zero-shot always compares with exactly one text per desk.

choices.text: Centroids, with sentences in place of averages
choices.why: Right. Each ticket goes to the nearest of five vectors, one per desk; only where those vectors come from is different.

choices.text: Keyword search for the desk names inside each ticket
choices.why: No word is matched: the bare names scored 39 by meaning, and returns or account appear in few of the tickets.

prompt: Order the three wordings `zeroshot.py` tried, from the most test tickets right to the fewest.
hint: One sentence listing what a desk covers did best.
items: A sentence describing what each desk covers
trap: The example messages are not in the middle: one particular ticket per desk scored worst, 35, below the bare names' 39.

prompt: Ana tries ten wordings of the five descriptions on the 50 test tickets and reports the best one's score, 45. What is wrong with that 45?
hint: Where did the choice of wording come from?

choices.text: The wording was chosen for its score on those same 50 tickets
choices.why: Right. Choosing among ten by their test score is learning from the test set through a person; the 45 will not hold on new tickets as it is.

choices.text: Nothing, because zero-shot uses no labels and so cannot learn from the test set
choices.why: The labels of the test set were used, to score each wording; the choice of wording carries what they said.

choices.text: A score of 45 is impossible without labelled training tickets
choices.why: Nothing makes it impossible; the best wording here already reached 43 with no training ticket.

choices.text: Each wording needs a test set of its own, of 50 different tickets
choices.why: The wordings can share a test set if none of them is chosen by it; the trouble is the choosing, not the sharing.

prompt: Sorting tickets with only a short text describing each desk, and no labelled example at all, is called ___ classification.
hint: The number of examples it needs.

prompt: In the confusion matrix `measure.py` printed, what does a number off the diagonal count?
hint: Rows are the real desk, columns the chosen one.

choices.text: Tickets from the training set that the classifier saw twice
choices.why: The matrix is built from the 50 test tickets only, each counted once.

choices.text: Tickets whose top probability was under 0.5
choices.why: The matrix counts labels, not probabilities; t027 is off the diagonal because its label was wrong, whatever its probability.

choices.text: Desks that received no tickets
choices.why: A desk with no tickets would show a column of zeros; every number is a count of tickets, on or off the diagonal.

choices.text: Tickets sent to a desk their label does not name
choices.why: Right. The row says where the ticket belongs and the column where it went; off the diagonal the two differ.

prompt: A classifier sends 12 tickets to the returns desk, and 9 of them really are returns. The test set has 10 returns tickets in all. What is the returns desk's precision, as a percentage?
hint: Precision asks about the tickets the desk received.

prompt: Match each measure in `measure.py`'s output to the question it answers.
hint: Two of them are about a single desk, from opposite sides.

pairs.right: How many of a desk's own tickets reached it?
How many tickets sent to a desk belong there?
Where did each desk's tickets go?
Precision and recall in one number

prompt: Two of the trained classifier's three mistakes, t024 and t027, are tickets that honestly fit two desks. What is the useful next step?
hint: Whose boundary is unclear: the model's or the team's?

choices.text: Add those tickets to the training set and measure again on the same 50
choices.why: Then the method has learned from its test tickets, and the new score measures memory of those two.

choices.text: Agree a rule for two-desk tickets and relabel before tuning
choices.why: Right. A classifier can only learn the boundaries the labels draw; if people would disagree on these tickets, the rule is the thing to fix first.

choices.text: Switch to an embedding model with more dimensions
choices.why: The model placed t027 between payments and shipping because it is about both; more dimensions do not settle which desk the team wants.

choices.text: Drop ambiguous tickets from the test set so that the score reflects the model
choices.why: Real queues contain ambiguous tickets; a test set without them reports a score the classifier will not get in use.

prompt: On another set of 50 test tickets, method A scores 47 and method B scores 46. What can you conclude about the two?
hint: One ticket is two points out of a hundred.

choices.text: A is two points better, so A should go into production
choices.why: Two points here is one ticket, well within what a different draw of 50 could change.

choices.text: B is better, because fewer right answers means less overfitting
choices.why: A lower test score is not evidence of anything good; overfitting shows as a test score below a training score, which nobody measured here.

choices.text: Nothing reliable about which is better: they differ by a single ticket
choices.why: Right. On another 50 tickets drawn the same way the order could flip; settling it needs more test data or cross-validation.

choices.text: A is at least as good as B on every desk
choices.why: A total says nothing about the desks; A could be better on three desks and worse on two, as the confusion matrix would show.

prompt: Put in order what happens when a new ticket is sorted with centroids, starting from the labelled training tickets.
hint: The centroids are ready before the new ticket arrives.
items: Average the vectors of each desk
Divide each average by its length
Score it against the five centroids and keep the highest
trap: Renormalising comes right after averaging and before any comparison; a centroid compared at its old length wins by length.

prompt: Which of these are true of k-nearest neighbours as `knn.py` does it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what it stores and what it computes.

choices.text: A newly sorted ticket can be used with no training run, by adding its vector
choices.why: Yes. Learning is appending: tomorrow's comparison simply includes one more row.

choices.text: Each decision can be traced back to the stored tickets that made it
choices.why: Yes. neighbours.py did exactly that for t021 and t054.

choices.text: It keeps every labelled vector and compares each new ticket with all of them
choices.why: Yes. That is its cost, and why at scale it becomes the search problem of lessons 11 and 15.

choices.text: It returns a probability for each desk alongside the label
choices.why: That is logistic regression's predict_proba; knn.py returns the winning label only.

choices.text: Changing a stored ticket's label means embedding every ticket again
choices.why: The vectors do not depend on the labels; changing a label changes one entry of ytr and nothing else.

prompt: Match each method to what a new ticket is compared with, or scored by.
hint: Count the vectors each one keeps.
